<color=#3366CC>archipelago</color> from the drops of water that fell from her spear" and in historic times, the spear was an item compared to
the sun and <color=#3366CC>solar deities</color>.
Differences in worship
Amaterasu, while primarily being the goddess of the sun, is also sometimes worshiped as having connections with
other aspects and forms of nature. Amaterasu can also be considered a goddess of the wind and typhoons alongside
her brother, and even possibly death. There are many connections between local legends in the Ise region with other
goddesses of nature, such as a nameless goddess of the underworld and sea. It is possible that Amaterasu's name
became associated with these legends in the Shinto religion as it grew throughout Japan.
One source interprets from the Heavenly Rock Cave myth that Amaterasu was seen as being responsible for the
normal cycle of day and night.
A historical myth holds that she painted the islands of Japan into being, alongside her siblings <color=#3366CC>Susanoo</color> and
Tsukuyomi.
In contrast, Amaterasu, while enshrined at other locations, also can be seen as the goddess that represents Japan and
its ethnicity. The many differences in Shinto religion and mythology can be due to how different local gods and beliefs
clashed. In the Meiji Era, the belief in Amaterasu fought against the Izumo belief in Ōkuninushi for spiritual control over
the land of Japan. During this time, the religious nature of Okininushi may have been changed to be included in Shinto
mythology. Osagawara Shouzo built shrines in other countries to mainly spread Japan's culture and Shinto religion. It,
however, was usually seen as the worshiping of Japan itself, rather than Amaterasu. Most of these colonial and
oversea shrines were destroyed after WWII.
Other worshiped forms
Snake
Outside of being worshiped as a sun goddess, some have argued that Amaterasu was once related to snakes. There
was a legend circulating among the Ise Priests that essentially described an encounter of Amaterasu sleeping with the
Saiō every night in the form of a snake or lizard, evidenced by fallen scales in the priestess' bed. This was recorded by
a medieval monk in his diary, which stated that "in ancient times Amaterasu was regarded as a snake deity or as a sun
deity." In the Ise kanjō, the god's snake form is considered an embodiment of the "three poisons", namely greed, anger,
and ignorance. Amaterasu is also linked to a snake cult, which is also tied to the theory that the initial gender of the
goddess was male.
Dragon
In general, some of these Amaterasu–dragon associations have been in reference to Japanese plays. One example
has been within the Chikubushima tradition in which the dragon goddess Benzaiten was the emanation of Amaterasu.
Following that, in the Japanese epic, Taiheki, one of the characters, Nitta Yoshisada, made comparisons with
Amaterasu and a dragon Ryūjin with the quote: "I have heard that the Sun Goddess of Ise … conceals her true being in
the august image of Vairocana, and that she has appeared in this world in the guise of a dragon god of the blue ocean."
Another tradition of the Heavenly Cave story depicts Amaterasu as a "dragon-fox" (shinko or tatsugitsune) during her
descent to the famed cave because it is a type of animal/<color=#3366CC>kami</color> that emits light from its entire body.
The connection between the fox, <color=#3366CC>Dakiniten</color>, and Amaterasu can also be seen in the Keiran Shūyōshū, which features
the following retelling of the myth of <color=#3366CC>Amaterasu's hiding</color>:
Question: What was the appearance of Amaterasu when she was hiding in the Rock-Cave of Heaven? Answer: Since
Amaterasu is the sun deity, she had the appearance of the sun-disc. Another tradition says: When Amaterasu retired
into the Rock-Cave of Heaven after her descent from Heaven (sic), she took on the appearance of a dragon-fox
(shinko). Uniquely among all animals, the dragon-fox is a kami that emits light from its body; this is the reason why she
took on this appearance.
Question: Why does the dragon-fox emit light?
Answer: The dragon-fox is an expedient body of Nyoirin <color=#3366CC>Kannon</color>. It takes the wish-fulfilling gem as its body, and is
therefore called King Cintāmani. ... Further, one tradition says that one becomes a king by revering the dragon-fox
because the dragon-fox is an expedient body of Amaterasu.
Commenting on the sokui kanjō, Bernard Faure writes:under the name "Fox King," Dakiniten became a manifestation of
the sun goddess Amaterasu, with whom the new emperor united during the enthronement ritual. [...] The Buddhist ritual
allowed the ruler to symbolically cross over the limits separating the human and animal realms to harness the wild and
properly superhuman energy of the "infrahuman" world, so as to gain full control of the human sphere.
In Japanese Buddhism
In Japanese Buddhism, Amaterasu was incorporated into a broad pantheon in which local <color=#3366CC>kami</color> were understood
through the doctrinal frameworks of honji suijaku theories of correspondence. Rather than being treated as an
independent creator deity, Amaterasu was interpreted as the “trace manifestation” (suijaku) of a Buddha, whose
“original ground” (honji) was identified variously depending on sectarian orientation and local cultic developments. The
trace-original ground framework allowed Buddhist scholastics to subordinate and encompass the sun goddess, along
with various other kami, within a universal Buddhist cosmos. Textual materials from the Nara and Heian periods show
that she came to function as a paradigmatic example of the capacity of Buddhas to appear as local deities for the sake
of guiding beings.
Within esoteric Buddhist traditions like Tendai and Shingon, Amaterasu was frequently correlated with Dainichi Nyorai
(Mahavariocana, "All Illuminator"), the cosmic Buddha who embodies the wisdom and luminosity. Shingon scholastics
like Dōhan directly identified the two figures. This identification of the two deities is also found in the writings of <color=#3366CC>Saigyō</color>
<color=#3366CC>Hōshi</color> who himself worshiped at the Grand Shrine of Ise, and in Kitabatake Chikafusa's Jinnō Shōtōki. These doctrinal
associations were supported by ritual elaborations at Shinto shrines, which were often attached to Buddhist temples,
where Buddhist clergy participated in ceremonies that merged esoteric liturgy with traditional shrine rites. Amaterasu
worship was also central to the syncretic <color=#3366CC>Ryōbu Shintō</color> sects, which drew extensively on Shingon Buddhist thought and
practice.
Worship of Amaterasu within Buddhist contexts was further intensified by her close connection to the <color=#3366CC>imperial house</color>.
Buddhist theorists, by linking her to Dainichi or other buddhas, reinforced the legitimacy of the imperial order within a
universal Buddhist cosmology. Court-sponsored rituals blended Buddhist and kami-centered elements, and pilgrimage
to Ise developed as a practice compatible with Buddhist soteriological aims. Medieval narratives, such as those found
in shrine-origin texts (engi), frequently emphasize that Amaterasu protects the state precisely because she is an
expedient manifestation of a higher Buddhist power. In these accounts, the prosperity of the realm and the stability of
the imperial lineage were understood as outcomes of the harmonious integration of Buddhist principle and kami
manifestation.
Local cults also adapted Amaterasu to specific devotional functions and freely mixed Shinto and Buddhist ideas. This
kind of religious syncretism is called Shinbutsu-shūgō and was a common feature of pre-modern Japanese religious
culture. The spread of syncretic institutions like jingūji (shrine-temples) provided an institutional basis for sustained
Buddhist interaction with the deity, including the recitation of sutras to honor the kami, the construction of Buddhist
icons representing their honji forms, and the performance of goma (fire rituals) intended to secure the divine protection.
These practices reflect the broader medieval understanding that kami could receive Buddhist offerings and respond
with worldly benefits, while ultimately serving the liberating activity of buddhas.
The situation changed significantly during the <color=#3366CC>Meiji period</color>, especially with the rise of nativist anti-Buddhist movements
that questioned or rejected Buddhist interpretive dominance, culminating in the rise of State Shinto and the official
separation of Shinto from Buddhism, shinbutsu bunri.
Relation to women's positions in early Japanese society
Because Amaterasu has the highest position among the Shinto deities, there has been debate on her influence and
relation to women's positions in early Japanese society. Some scholars have argued that the goddess' presence and
high stature within the kami system could suggest that early rulers in Japan were female. Others have argued the
goddess' presence implies strong influences female priests had in Japanese politics and religion.
In Japanese new religions
Amaterasu is the main deity, or one of the main deities, worshipped in various Japanese new religions, including
Kurozumikyō, Shintō Tenkōkyo, Tenshō Kōtai Jingūkyō, and Kōmyō Kamu Tama Jingū.
Western world
The Western world, also known as the West, primarily refers to various <color=#3366CC>nations</color> and <color=#3366CC>states</color> in Europe, Northern
America, and <color=#3366CC>Australasia</color>; with some debate as to whether those in the former Soviet Union and <color=#3366CC>Latin America</color> also
constitute the West. The Western world likewise is called the Occident in contrast to the <color=#3366CC>Eastern world</color> known as the
<color=#3366CC>Orient</color>. Definitions of the "Western world" vary according to context and perspectives; the West is an evolving concept
made up of cultural, political, and economic synergy among diverse groups of people, and not a rigid region with fixed
borders and members.
Ancient Greece and Rome are widely regarded as the birthplaces of Western civilization. A geographical concept of the
West started to take shape in the 4th century CE when <color=#3366CC>Constantine</color>, the first Christian Roman emperor, divided the
Roman Empire between the Greek East and Latin West. The <color=#3366CC>East Roman Empire</color>, later called the <color=#3366CC>Byzantine Empire</color>,
continued for a millennium, while the <color=#3366CC>West Roman Empire</color> lasted for only about a century and a half. Significant
theological and ecclesiastical differences led Western Europeans to consider the Christians in the Byzantine Empire as
heretics. In 1054 CE, when the church in Rome <color=#3366CC>excommunicated</color> the <color=#3366CC>patriarch of Byzantium</color>, the politico-religious
division between the <color=#3366CC>Western church</color> and <color=#3366CC>Eastern church</color> culminated in the Great Schism or the <color=#3366CC>East–West Schism</color>.
Even though friendly relations continued between the two parts of <color=#3366CC>Christendom</color> for some time, the <color=#3366CC>crusades</color> made the
schism definitive with hostility. The West during these crusades tried to capture trade routes to the East and failed, it
instead discovered the <color=#3366CC>Americas</color>. In the aftermath of the <color=#3366CC>European colonization of the Americas</color>, primarily involving
<color=#3366CC>Western European</color> powers, an idea of the "Western" world, as an inheritor of Latin Christendom emerged. According to
the <color=#3366CC>Oxford English Dictionary</color>, the earliest reference to the term "Western world" was from 1586, found in the writings of
William Warner.
The countries that are considered constituents of the West vary according to perspective rather than their geographical
location. Countries like Australia and New Zealand, located in the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Hemisphere</color> are included in modern
definitions of the Western world, as these regions and others like them have been significantly influenced by the
<color=#3366CC>British</color>—derived from <color=#3366CC>colonization</color>, and immigration of Europeans—factors that grounded such countries to the West.
Depending on the context and the historical period in question, <color=#3366CC>Russia</color> was sometimes seen as a part of the West, and
at other times juxtaposed with it, as well as endorsing anti-Western sentiment. The <color=#3366CC>United States</color> became more
prominently featured in the conceptualizations of the West as it rose as a <color=#3366CC>great power</color>, amidst the development of
communication–transportation technologies like the <color=#3366CC>telegraph</color> and <color=#3366CC>railroads</color> "shrinking" the distance between both the
<color=#3366CC>Atlantic Ocean</color> shores.
At some times between the 18th century and the mid-20th century, prominent countries in the West, such as the United

States, <color=#3366CC>Canada</color>, <color=#3366CC>Brazil</color>, <color=#3366CC>Argentina</color>, <color=#3366CC>Australia</color>, and <color=#3366CC>New Zealand</color>, have been envisioned by some as ethnocracies for
<color=#3366CC>Whites</color>. <color=#3366CC>Racism</color> is claimed as a contributing factor to Western European colonization of the <color=#3366CC>New World</color>, which today
constitutes much of the geographical Western world-split between <color=#3366CC>Global North and Global South</color>. Starting from the
late 1960s, certain parts of the Western world have become notable for their diversity due to immigration and changes
in fertility rates. The idea of "the West" over the course of time has evolved from a directional concept to a
socio-political concept, temporalized and rendered as a concept of the future bestowed with notions of progress and
modernity.
Introduction
The origins of Western civilization can be traced back to the <color=#3366CC>ancient Mediterranean world</color>. <color=#3366CC>Ancient Greece</color> and <color=#3366CC>Ancient</color>
<color=#3366CC>Rome</color> are generally considered to be the birthplaces of Western civilization—Greece having heavily influenced

Rome—the former due to its impact on <color=#3366CC>philosophy</color>, <color=#3366CC>democracy</color>, <color=#3366CC>science</color>, <color=#3366CC>aesthetics</color>, as well as <color=#3366CC>building designs and</color>

<color=#3366CC>proportions and architecture</color>; the latter due to its influence on <color=#3366CC>art</color>, <color=#3366CC>law</color>, <color=#3366CC>warfare</color>, <color=#3366CC>governance</color>, <color=#3366CC>republicanism</color>, engineering
and religion. Western Civilization is also closely associated with <color=#3366CC>Christianity</color>, the dominant religion in the West, with
roots in <color=#3366CC>Greco</color>-Roman and <color=#3366CC>Jewish thought</color>. <color=#3366CC>Christian ethics</color>, drawing from the ethical and moral principles of its
historical roots in <color=#3366CC>Judaism</color>, has played a pivotal role in shaping the foundational framework of Western societies. Earlier
civilizations, such as the <color=#3366CC>ancient Egyptians</color> and <color=#3366CC>Mesopotamians</color>, had also significantly influenced Western civilization
through their advancements in writing, law codes, and societal structures. The convergence of Greek-Roman and
Judeo-Christian influences in shaping Western civilization has led certain scholars to characterize it as emerging from
the legacies of <color=#3366CC>Athens</color> and <color=#3366CC>Jerusalem</color>, or Athens, Jerusalem and <color=#3366CC>Rome</color>.
In ancient Greece and Rome, individuals identified primarily as subjects of states, city-states, or empires, rather than as
members of Western civilization. The distinct identification of Western civilization began to crystallize with the rise of
Christianity during the Late Roman Empire. In this period, peoples in Europe started to perceive themselves as part of
a unique civilization, differentiating from others like <color=#3366CC>Islam</color>, giving rise to the concept of Western civilization. By the 15th
century, <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color> intellectuals solidified this concept, associating Western civilization not only with Christianity but
also with the intellectual and political achievements of the ancient Greeks and Romans.
Historians, such as Carroll Quigley in "The Evolution of Civilizations", contend that Western civilization was born around
AD 500, after the <color=#3366CC>fall of the Western Roman Empire</color>, leaving a vacuum for new ideas to flourish that were impossible in
Classical societies. In either view, between the fall of the Western Roman Empire and the Renaissance, the West (or
those regions that would later become the heartland of the culturally "western sphere") experienced a period of decline,
and then readaptation, reorientation and considerable renewed material, technological and political development.
<color=#3366CC>Classical</color> culture of the <color=#3366CC>ancient Western world</color> was partly preserved during this period due to the survival of the <color=#3366CC>Eastern</color>
<color=#3366CC>Roman Empire</color> and the introduction of the <color=#3366CC>Catholic Church</color>; it was also greatly expanded by the Arab importation of
both the <color=#3366CC>Ancient Greco-Roman</color> and new technology through the Arabs from India and China to Europe.
Since the Renaissance, the West evolved beyond the influence of the ancient Greeks and Romans and the Islamic
world, due to the successful <color=#3366CC>Second Agricultural</color>, Commercial, <color=#3366CC>Scientific</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Industrial</color> revolutions (propellers of
<color=#3366CC>modern banking</color> concepts). The West rose further with the 18th century's <color=#3366CC>Age of Enlightenment</color> and through the <color=#3366CC>Age of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Exploration</color>'s expansion of peoples of European empires in the 18th and 19th centuries, particularly the globe-spanning
colonial empires of Western Europe. Numerous times, this expansion was accompanied by Catholic <color=#3366CC>missionaries</color>, who
attempted to proselytize Christianity.
In the modern era, Western culture has undergone further transformation through the <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color>, Ages of <color=#3366CC>Discovery</color>
and <color=#3366CC>Enlightenment</color>, and the Industrial and <color=#3366CC>Scientific Revolutions</color>. The widespread influence of Western culture
extended globally through <color=#3366CC>imperialism</color>, <color=#3366CC>colonialism</color>, and Christianization by Western powers from the <color=#3366CC>15th to 20th</color>
<color=#3366CC>centuries</color>. This influence persists through the exportation of mass culture, a phenomenon often referred to as
Westernization.
There was debate among some in the 1960s as to whether <color=#3366CC>Latin America</color> as a whole is in a category of its own.
Culture
Historical divisions
The west of the Mediterranean region during antiquity
The geopolitical divisions in Europe that created a concept of East and West originated in the <color=#3366CC>ancient</color> tyrannical and
imperialistic Graeco-Roman times. The Eastern <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean</color> was home to the highly urbanized cultures that had
<color=#3366CC>Greek</color> as their common language (owing to the older empire of <color=#3366CC>Alexander the Great</color> and of the <color=#3366CC>Hellenistic successors</color>),
whereas the West was much more rural in its character and more readily adopted Latin as its common language. After
the fall of the Western Roman Empire and the beginning of medieval times (or <color=#3366CC>Middle Ages</color>), Western and Central
Europe were substantially cut off from the East, where <color=#3366CC>Byzantine</color> Greek culture and <color=#3366CC>Eastern Christianity</color> became
founding influences in the Eastern European world such as the East and South Slavic peoples.
<color=#3366CC>Roman Catholic</color> Western and Central Europe thus maintained a distinct identity, particularly as it began to redevelop
during the Renaissance. Even following the Protestant <color=#3366CC>Reformation</color>, Protestant Europe continued to see itself as more
tied to Roman Catholic Europe than other parts of the perceived "civilized world". Use of the term West as a specific
cultural and geopolitical term developed over the course of the <color=#3366CC>Age of Exploration</color> as Europe spread its culture to other
parts of the world. Roman Catholics were the first major religious group to migrate to the <color=#3366CC>New World</color>, as settlers in the

colonies of <color=#3366CC>Spain</color> and <color=#3366CC>Portugal</color> (and later, <color=#3366CC>France</color>) belonged to that faith. <color=#3366CC>English</color> and <color=#3366CC>Dutch</color> colonies, on the other
hand, tended to be more religiously diverse. Settlers to these colonies included <color=#3366CC>Anglicans</color>, Dutch <color=#3366CC>Calvinists</color>, English
<color=#3366CC>Puritans</color> and other nonconformists, English Catholics, Scottish <color=#3366CC>Presbyterians</color>, French <color=#3366CC>Huguenots</color>, German and
Swedish <color=#3366CC>Lutherans</color>, as well as <color=#3366CC>Quakers</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mennonites</color>, <color=#3366CC>Amish</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Moravians</color>.
Ancient Roman world (6th century BC – AD 395–476)
<color=#3366CC>Ancient Rome</color> (6th century BC – AD 476) is a term to describe the ancient Roman society that conquered Central Italy
assimilating the Italian Etruscan culture, growing from the Latium region since about the 8th century BC, to a massive
empire straddling the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean Sea</color>. In its 10-centuries territorial expansion, <color=#3366CC>Roman civilization</color> shifted from a
small <color=#3366CC>monarchy</color> (753–509 BC), to a <color=#3366CC>republic</color> (509–27 BC), into an <color=#3366CC>autocratic</color> empire (27 BC – AD 476). Its Empire
came to dominate Western, Central and Southeastern Europe, Northern Africa and, becoming an autocratic Empire a
vast Middle Eastern area, when it ended. Conquest was enforced using the <color=#3366CC>Roman legions</color> and then through <color=#3366CC>cultural</color>
<color=#3366CC>assimilation</color> by eventual recognition of some form of Roman citizenship's privileges. Nonetheless, despite its great
legacy, a number of factors led to the eventual decline and ultimately <color=#3366CC>fall of the Roman Empire</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>Roman Empire</color> succeeded the approximately 500-year-old <color=#3366CC>Roman Republic</color> (c. 510–30 BC). In 350 years, from the
successful and deadliest <color=#3366CC>war</color> with the <color=#3366CC>Phoenicians</color> which began in 218 BC to the rule of <color=#3366CC>Emperor Hadrian</color> by AD 117,
ancient Rome expanded up to twenty-five times its area. The same time passed again before its fall in AD 476. Rome
had expanded long before the empire reached its zenith with the conquest of <color=#3366CC>Dacia</color> in AD 106 (modern-day <color=#3366CC>Romania</color>)
under Emperor Trajan. During its territorial peak, the Roman Empire controlled about 5000000 km2 of land surface and
had a population of 100 million. From the time of Caesar (100–44 BC) to the Fall of the Western Roman Empire, Rome
dominated <color=#3366CC>Southern Europe</color>, the Mediterranean coast of <color=#3366CC>Northern Africa</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Levant</color>, including the ancient trade
<color=#3366CC>routes</color> with population living outside. Ancient Rome has contributed greatly to the development of law, war, art,
literature, architecture, technology and language in the Western world, and its <color=#3366CC>history</color> continues to have a major
influence on the world today. The <color=#3366CC>Latin language</color> has been the base from which <color=#3366CC>Romance languages</color> evolved and it
has been the official language of the <color=#3366CC>Catholic Church</color> and all Catholic religious ceremonies all over Europe until 1967,
as well as one of, or the official language of countries such as Italy and Poland (9th–18th centuries).
In AD 395, a few decades before its Western collapse, the Roman Empire formally split into a <color=#3366CC>Western</color> and an <color=#3366CC>Eastern</color>
one, each with their own emperors, capitals, and governments, although ostensibly they still belonged to one formal
Empire. The <color=#3366CC>Western Roman Empire</color> provinces eventually were replaced by <color=#3366CC>Northern European</color> <color=#3366CC>Germanic</color> ruled
kingdoms in the 5th century due to <color=#3366CC>civil wars, corruption, and devastating Germanic invasions</color> from such tribes as the

<color=#3366CC>Huns</color>, <color=#3366CC>Goths</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Franks</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Vandals</color> by their late <color=#3366CC>expansion</color> throughout Europe. The three-day Visigoths's <color=#3366CC>AD 410</color>
<color=#3366CC>sack of Rome</color> who had been raiding Greece not long before, a shocking time for Greco-Romans, was the first time after
almost 800 years that Rome had fallen to a foreign enemy, and <color=#3366CC>St. Jerome</color>, living in Bethlehem at the time, wrote that
"The City which had taken the whole world was itself taken." There followed the sack of AD 455 lasting 14 days, this
time conducted by the Vandals, retaining Rome's eternal spirit through the <color=#3366CC>Holy See of Rome</color> (the Latin Church) for
centuries to come. The ancient <color=#3366CC>Barbarian</color> tribes, often composed of well-trained Roman soldiers paid by Rome to guard
the extensive borders, had become militarily sophisticated "Romanized barbarians", and mercilessly slaughtered the
Romans conquering their Western territories while looting their possessions.
The Roman Empire is where the idea of "the West" began to emerge.
The <color=#3366CC>Eastern Roman Empire</color>, governed from <color=#3366CC>Constantinople</color>, is usually referred to as the <color=#3366CC>Byzantine Empire</color> after AD
476, the traditional date for the fall of the Roman Empire and beginning of the <color=#3366CC>Early Middle Ages</color>. The survival of the
Eastern Roman Empire protected Roman legal and cultural traditions, combining them with Greek and Christian
elements, for another thousand years. The name Byzantine Empire was first used centuries later, after the Byzantine
Empire ended. The dissolution of the Western half, nominally ended in AD 476, but in truth a long process that ended
by the rise of Catholic <color=#3366CC>Gaul</color> (modern-day <color=#3366CC>France</color>) ruling from around the year AD 800, left only the Eastern Roman
Empire alive. The Eastern half continued to think of itself as the Roman Empire. The inhabitants called themselves
Romans because the term "Roman" was meant to signify all <color=#3366CC>Christians</color>. The Pope crowned <color=#3366CC>Charlemagne</color> as Emperor
of the Romans of the newly established <color=#3366CC>Holy Roman Empire</color>, and the West began thinking in terms of Western Latins
living in the old Western Empire, and Eastern Greeks (those inside the Roman remnant of the old Eastern Empire).
The birth of the European West during the Middle Ages
In the early 4th century, the central focus of power was on two separate imperial legacies within the Roman Empire: the
older <color=#3366CC>Aegean Sea</color> <color=#3366CC>Greek</color> heritage (of <color=#3366CC>Classical Greece</color>) in the Eastern Mediterranean, and the newer most successful
<color=#3366CC>Tyrrhenian Sea</color> <color=#3366CC>Latin</color> heritage (of Ancient Latium and Tuscany) in the Western Mediterranean. A turning point was

<color=#3366CC>Constantine the Great</color>'s decision to establish the city of <color=#3366CC>Constantinople</color> (today's <color=#3366CC>Istanbul</color>) in modern-day <color=#3366CC>Turkey</color> as the
"New Rome" when he picked it as capital of his Empire (later called "<color=#3366CC>Byzantine Empire</color>" by modern historians) in AD
This internal conflict of legacies had possibly emerged since the <color=#3366CC>assassination of Julius Caesar</color> three centuries earlier,
when Roman imperialism had just been born with the Roman Republic becoming "Roman Empire", but reached its
zenith during 3rd century's many internal civil wars. This is the time when the <color=#3366CC>Huns</color> (part of the ancient Eastern
European tribes named barbarians by the Romans) from modern-day <color=#3366CC>Hungary</color> penetrated into the Dalmatian
(modern-day <color=#3366CC>Croatia</color>) region then originating in the following 150 years in the Roman Empire officially splitting in two
halves. Also the time of the formal acceptance of Christianity as Empire's <color=#3366CC>religious</color> policy, when the Emperors began
actively banning and fighting previous <color=#3366CC>pagan religions</color>.
The Eastern Roman Empire included lands south-west of the <color=#3366CC>Black Sea</color> and bordering on the Eastern Mediterranean
and parts of the <color=#3366CC>Adriatic Sea</color>. This division into Eastern and Western Roman Empires was later reflected in the
administration of the Roman Catholic and Eastern Greek Orthodox churches, with Rome and Constantinople debating
over whether either city was the capital of <color=#3366CC>Western religion</color>.
As the <color=#3366CC>Eastern (Orthodox)</color> and Western (Catholic) churches spread their influence, the line between Eastern and
Western Christianity was moving. Its movement was affected by the influence of the Byzantine empire and the
fluctuating power and influence of the Catholic church in Rome. The geographic line of religious division approximately
followed a line of cultural divide.
In AD 800 under <color=#3366CC>Charlemagne</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Early Medieval</color> Franks established an empire that was recognized by the <color=#3366CC>Pope</color> in
Rome as the <color=#3366CC>Holy Roman Empire</color> (Latin Christian revival of the ancient Roman Empire, under perpetual Germanic rule
from AD 962) inheriting ancient Roman Empire's prestige but offending the Eastern Roman Emperor in Constantinople,
and leading to the <color=#3366CC>Crusades</color> and the East–West Schism. The crowning of the Emperor by the Pope led to the
assumption that the highest power was the <color=#3366CC>papal hierarchy</color>, quintessential Roman Empire's spiritual heritage authority,
establishing then, until the Protestant Reformation, the civilization of <color=#3366CC>Western Christendom</color>.
The earliest concept of Europe as a cultural sphere (instead of simple geographic term) is believed to have been
formed by <color=#3366CC>Alcuin of York</color> during the <color=#3366CC>Carolingian Renaissance</color> of the 9th century, but was limited to the territories that
practised Western Christianity at the time.
The Latin Church of western and central Europe split with the eastern <color=#3366CC>Greek</color> patriarchates in the Christian <color=#3366CC>East–West</color>
<color=#3366CC>Schism</color>, also known as the "Great Schism", during the Gregorian Reforms (calling for a more central status of the
Roman Catholic Church Institution), three months after <color=#3366CC>Pope Leo IX</color>'s death in April 1054. Following the 1054 <color=#3366CC>Great</color>
<color=#3366CC>Schism</color>, both the Western Church and <color=#3366CC>Eastern</color> Church continued to consider themselves uniquely orthodox and
catholic. <color=#3366CC>Augustine</color> wrote in On True Religion: "Religion is to be sought... only among those who are called Catholic or
orthodox Christians, that is, guardians of truth and followers of right." Over time, the Western Christianity gradually
identified with the "Catholic" label, and people of Western Europe gradually associated the "Orthodox" label with
<color=#3366CC>Eastern Christianity</color> (although in some languages the "Catholic" label is not necessarily identified with the Western
Church). This was in note of the fact that both Catholic and Orthodox were in use as ecclesiastical adjectives as early
as the 2nd and 4th centuries respectively. Meanwhile, the extent of both Christendoms expanded, as Germanic
peoples, Bohemia, Poland, Hungary, Scandinavia, Finnic peoples, Baltic peoples, British Isles and the other
non-Christian lands of the northwest were converted by the Western Church, while Eastern Slavic peoples, Bulgaria,
Serbia, Montenegro, Russian territories, Vlachs and Georgia were converted by the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Orthodox Church</color>.
In 1071, the Byzantine army was defeated by the <color=#3366CC>Muslim</color> <color=#3366CC>Turco-Persians</color> of medieval <color=#3366CC>Asia</color>, resulting in the loss of most
of <color=#3366CC>Asia Minor</color>. The situation was a serious threat to the future of the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Orthodox</color> <color=#3366CC>Byzantine Empire</color>. The Emperor
sent a plea to the <color=#3366CC>Pope</color> in Rome to send military aid to restore the lost territories to Christian rule. The result was a
series of western European military campaigns into the eastern Mediterranean, known as the Crusades. Unfortunately
for the Byzantines, the crusaders (belonging to the members of nobility from France, German territories, the Low
countries, England and Italy) had no allegiance to the Byzantine Emperor and established their own states in the
conquered regions, <color=#3366CC>including the heart of the Byzantine Empire</color>.
The Holy Roman Empire would dissolve on 6 August 1806, after the <color=#3366CC>French Revolution</color> and the creation of the
<color=#3366CC>Confederation of the Rhine</color> by <color=#3366CC>Napoleon</color>.
The decline of the Byzantine Empire (13th–15th centuries) began with the <color=#3366CC>Latin Christian</color> <color=#3366CC>Fourth Crusade</color> in AD
1202–04, considered to be one of the most important events, solidifying the <color=#3366CC>schism</color> between the <color=#3366CC>Christian</color> churches of
<color=#3366CC>Greek</color> Byzantine Rite and <color=#3366CC>Latin</color> Roman Rite. An anti-Western riot in 1182 broke out in <color=#3366CC>Constantinople</color> targeting Latins.
The extremely wealthy (after previous <color=#3366CC>Crusades</color>) <color=#3366CC>Venetians</color> in particular made a successful attempt to maintain control
over the coast of <color=#3366CC>Catholic</color> present-day Croatia (specifically the Dalmatia, a region of interest to the <color=#3366CC>maritime</color> medieval
Venetian Republic moneylenders and its rivals, such as the Republic of Genoa) rebelling against the Venetian
economic domination. What followed dealt an irrevocable blow to the already weakened Byzantine Empire with the
<color=#3366CC>Crusader army's sack of Constantinople</color> in April 1204, capital of the <color=#3366CC>Greek Christian</color>-controlled <color=#3366CC>Byzantine Empire</color>,
described as one of the most profitable and disgraceful sacks of a city in history. This paved the way for Muslim
conquests in <color=#3366CC>present-day Turkey</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Balkans</color> in the coming centuries (only a handful of the Crusaders followed to
the stated destination thereafter, the <color=#3366CC>Holy Land</color>). The geographical identity of the Balkans is historically known as a
crossroads of cultures, a juncture between the <color=#3366CC>Latin</color> and <color=#3366CC>Greek</color> bodies of the <color=#3366CC>Roman Empire</color>, the destination of a
massive influx of pagans (meaning "non-Christians") <color=#3366CC>Bulgars</color> and <color=#3366CC>Slavs</color>, an area where <color=#3366CC>Catholic</color> and <color=#3366CC>Orthodox</color>
Christianity met, as well as the meeting point between <color=#3366CC>Islam</color> and Christianity. The Papal Inquisition was established in
AD 1229 on a permanent basis, run largely by clergymen in Rome, and abolished six centuries later. Before AD 1100,
the <color=#3366CC>Catholic Church suppressed</color> what they believed to be heresy, usually through a system of ecclesiastical
proscription or imprisonment, but without using torture, and seldom resorting to executions.
This very profitable <color=#3366CC>Central European</color> Fourth Crusade had prompted the 14th century <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color> (translated as
'Rebirth') of Italian city-states including the <color=#3366CC>Papal States</color>, on eve of the Protestant Reformation and
<color=#3366CC>Counter-Reformation</color> (which established the Roman Inquisition to succeed the Medieval Inquisition). There followed the
discovery of the American continent, and consequent dissolution of West Christendom as even a theoretical unitary
political body, later resulting in the religious <color=#3366CC>Eighty Years War</color> (1568–1648) and <color=#3366CC>Thirty Years War</color> (1618–1648) between
various Protestant and Catholic states of the <color=#3366CC>Holy Roman Empire</color> (and emergence of <color=#3366CC>religiously diverse</color> confessions).
In this context, the Protestant Reformation (1517) may be viewed as a schism within the Catholic Church. German
monk <color=#3366CC>Martin Luther</color>, in the wake of precursors, broke with the pope and with the emperor by the Catholic Church's
abusive commercialization of <color=#3366CC>indulgences</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Late Medieval Period</color>, backed by many of the German princes and
helped by the development of the <color=#3366CC>printing press</color>, in an attempt to reform corruption within the church.
Both these religious wars ended with the <color=#3366CC>Peace of Westphalia</color> (1648), which enshrined the concept of the <color=#3366CC>nation-state</color>,
and the principle of absolute <color=#3366CC>national sovereignty</color> in <color=#3366CC>international law</color>. As European influence spread across the globe,
these Westphalian principles, especially the concept of sovereign states, became central to international law and to the
prevailing world order.
Expansion of the West: the Era of Colonialism (15th–20th centuries)
In the 13th and 14th centuries, a number of European travelers, many of them Christian <color=#3366CC>missionaries</color>, had sought to
cultivate trading with Asia and <color=#3366CC>Africa</color>. With the Crusades came the relative contraction of the Orthodox Byzantine's
large silk industry in favor of Catholic Western Europe and the rise of <color=#3366CC>Western Papacy</color>. The most famous of these
merchant travelers pursuing <color=#3366CC>East–west trade</color> was Venetian <color=#3366CC>Marco Polo</color>. But these journeys had little permanent effect
on east–west trade because of a series of political developments in Asia in the last decades of the 14th century, which
put an end to further European exploration of Asia: namely the new <color=#3366CC>Ming</color> rulers were found to be unreceptive of
religious proselytism by European missionaries and merchants. Meanwhile, the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman</color> Turks consolidated control
over the eastern <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean</color>, closing off key overland trade routes.
The <color=#3366CC>Portuguese</color> spearheaded the drive to find oceanic routes that would provide cheaper and easier access to South
and East Asian goods, by advancements in maritime technology such as the <color=#3366CC>caravel</color> ship introduced in the mid-1400s.
The charting of oceanic routes between East and West began with the unprecedented voyages of Portuguese and
<color=#3366CC>Spanish</color> sea captains. In 1492, <color=#3366CC>European colonialism</color> expanded across the globe with the <color=#3366CC>exploring voyage</color> of
merchant, navigator, and Hispano-Italian colonizer <color=#3366CC>Christopher Columbus</color>. Such voyages were influenced by medieval
European adventurers after the European <color=#3366CC>spice trade</color> with Asia, who had journeyed overland to the Far East
contributing to geographical knowledge of parts of the Asian continent. They are of enormous significance in Western
history as they marked the beginning of the European exploration, <color=#3366CC>colonization</color> and exploitation of <color=#3366CC>the American</color>

<color=#3366CC>continents</color> and their <color=#3366CC>native inhabitants</color>. The <color=#3366CC>European colonization of the Americas</color> led to the <color=#3366CC>Atlantic slave trade</color>
between the 1490s and the 1800s, which also contributed to the development of African intertribal warfare and racist
ideology. Before the abolition of its slave trade in 1807, the <color=#3366CC>British Empire</color> alone (which had started colonial efforts <color=#3366CC>in</color>
<color=#3366CC>1578</color>, almost a century after Portuguese and Spanish empires) was responsible for the transportation of 3.5 million
African slaves to the Americas, a third of all slaves transported across the Atlantic. The <color=#3366CC>Holy Roman Empire</color> was
dissolved in 1806 by the <color=#3366CC>French Revolutionary Wars</color>; abolition of the Roman Catholic Inquisition followed.
Due to the reach of these empires, Western institutions expanded throughout the world. This process of influence (and
imposition) began with the <color=#3366CC>voyages of discovery</color>, <color=#3366CC>colonization, conquest, and exploitation</color> of <color=#3366CC>Portugal</color> enforced as well
by papal bulls in 1450s (by the <color=#3366CC>fall of the Byzantine Empire</color>), granting Portugal navigation, war and trade monopoly for
any newly discovered lands, and competing <color=#3366CC>Spanish</color> navigators. It continued with the rise of the <color=#3366CC>Dutch East India</color>
<color=#3366CC>Company</color> by the destabilizing Spanish <color=#3366CC>discovery of the New World</color>, and the creation and expansion of the <color=#3366CC>English</color> and
<color=#3366CC>French</color> colonial empires, and others. Even after demands for self-determination from subject peoples within Western
empires were met with <color=#3366CC>decolonization</color>, these institutions persisted. One specific example was the requirement that
<color=#3366CC>post-colonial</color> societies were made to form nation-states (in the Western tradition), which often created arbitrary
boundaries and borders that did not necessarily represent a whole nation, people, or culture (as in much of Africa), and
are often the cause of international conflicts and friction even to this day. Although not part of Western colonization
process proper, following the <color=#3366CC>Middle Ages</color> Western culture in fact entered other global-spanning cultures during the
colonial 15th–20th centuries. Historically <color=#3366CC>colonialism</color> had been justified with the values of <color=#3366CC>individualism</color> and
<color=#3366CC>enlightenment</color>.
The concepts of a world of <color=#3366CC>nation-states</color> born by the <color=#3366CC>Peace of Westphalia</color> in 1648, coupled with the ideologies of the
Enlightenment, the coming of <color=#3366CC>modernity</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Scientific Revolution</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Industrial Revolution</color>, would produce
powerful social transformations, political and <color=#3366CC>economic</color> institutions that have come to <color=#3366CC>influence</color> (or been imposed upon)
most nations of the world today. Historians agree that the Industrial Revolution has been one of the most important
events in history.
The course of <color=#3366CC>three centuries</color> since Christopher Columbus' late 15th century's voyages, of <color=#3366CC>deportation of slaves</color> from
Africa and <color=#3366CC>British</color> dominant northern-<color=#3366CC>Atlantic</color> location, later developed into modern-day <color=#3366CC>United States of America</color>,
evolving from the ratification of the <color=#3366CC>Constitution of the United States</color> by thirteen States on the North American East
Coast before end of the 18th century.
Enlightenment (17th–18th centuries)
Eric Voegelin described the 18th century as one where "the sentiment grows that one age has come to its close and
that a new age of Western civilization is about to be born". According to Voeglin the Enlightenment (also called the <color=#3366CC>Age</color>
<color=#3366CC>of Reason</color>) represents the "atrophy of Christian transcendental experiences and [seeks] to enthrone the <color=#3366CC>Newtonian</color>
method of science as the only valid method of arriving at truth". Its precursors were <color=#3366CC>John Milton</color> and <color=#3366CC>Baruch Spinoza</color>.
Meeting <color=#3366CC>Galileo</color> in 1638 left an enduring impact on John Milton and influenced Milton's great work Areopagitica, where
he warns that, without <color=#3366CC>free speech</color>, inquisitorial forces will impose "an undeserved thraldom upon learning".
The achievements of the 17th century included the invention of the <color=#3366CC>telescope</color> and acceptance of <color=#3366CC>heliocentrism</color>.
Eighteenth-century scholars continued to refine <color=#3366CC>Newton's theory of gravitation</color>, notably <color=#3366CC>Leonhard Euler</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pierre Louis</color>

<color=#3366CC>Maupertuis</color>, Alexis-Claude Clairaut, <color=#3366CC>Jean Le Rond d'Alembert</color>, <color=#3366CC>Joseph-Louis Lagrange</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pierre-Simon de Laplace</color>.
Laplace's five-volume Treatise on Celestial Mechanics is one of the great works of 18th-century Newtonianism.
<color=#3366CC>Astronomy</color> gained in prestige as new observatories were funded by governments and more powerful telescopes
developed, leading to the discovery of new planets, <color=#3366CC>asteroids</color>, <color=#3366CC>nebulae</color> and <color=#3366CC>comets</color>, and paving the way for
improvements in <color=#3366CC>navigation</color> and <color=#3366CC>cartography</color>. Astronomy became the second most popular scientific profession, after
<color=#3366CC>medicine</color>.
A common metanarrative of the Enlightenment is the "secularization theory". Modernity, as understood within the
framework, means a total break with the past. Innovation and science are the good, representing the modern values of
<color=#3366CC>rationalism</color>, while faith is ruled by superstition and traditionalism. Inspired by the Scientific Revolution, the
Enlightenment embodied the ideals of improvement and progress. <color=#3366CC>Descartes</color> and <color=#3366CC>Isaac Newton</color> were regarded as
exemplars of human intellectual achievement. <color=#3366CC>Condorcet</color> wrote about the progress of humanity in the Sketch for a
Historical Picture of the Progress of the Human Mind (1794), from primitive society to <color=#3366CC>agrarianism</color>, the invention of
writing, the later invention of the <color=#3366CC>printing press</color> and the advancement to "the Period when the Sciences and Philosophy
threw off the Yoke of Authority".
French writer <color=#3366CC>Pierre Bayle</color> denounced Spinoza as a <color=#3366CC>pantheist</color> (thereby accusing him of <color=#3366CC>atheism</color>). Bayle's criticisms
garnered much attention for Spinoza. The pantheism controversy in the late 18th century saw <color=#3366CC>Gotthold Lessing</color>
attacked by Friedrich Heinrich Jacobi over support for Spinoza's pantheism. Lessing was defended by Moses
Mendelssohn, although Mendelssohn diverged from pantheism to follow <color=#3366CC>Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz</color> in arguing that God
and the world were not of the same substance (equivalency). Spinoza was excommunicated from the Dutch Sephardic
community, but for Jews who sought out Jewish sources to guide their own path to secularism, Spinoza was as
important as Voltaire and Kant.
19th century
In the early 19th century, the systematic <color=#3366CC>urbanization</color> process (migration from villages in search of jobs in
manufacturing centers) had begun, and the concentration of labor into factories led to the rise in the population of the
towns. World population had been rising as well. It is estimated to have first reached one billion in 1804. Also, the new
philosophical movement later known as <color=#3366CC>Romanticism</color> originated, in the wake of the previous Age of Reason of the
1600s and the <color=#3366CC>Enlightenment</color> of 1700s. These are seen as fostering the 19th century Western worlds sustained
economic development. Before the urbanization and industrialization of the 1800s, demand for <color=#3366CC>oriental</color> goods such as

<color=#3366CC>porcelain</color>, <color=#3366CC>silk</color>, <color=#3366CC>spices</color> and <color=#3366CC>tea</color> remained the driving force behind European imperialism in Asia, and (with the important
exception of British East India Company rule in India) the European stake in Asia remained confined largely to trading
stations and strategic outposts necessary to protect trade. <color=#3366CC>Industrialization</color>, however, dramatically increased European
demand for Asian raw materials; and the severe Long Depression of the 1870s provoked a scramble for new markets
for European industrial products and financial services in Africa, the Americas, Eastern Europe, and especially in Asia
(Western powers exploited their advantages in <color=#3366CC>China</color> for example by the Opium Wars). This resulted in the "<color=#3366CC>New</color>
<color=#3366CC>Imperialism</color>", which saw a shift in focus from trade and indirect rule to formal colonial control of vast overseas territories
ruled as political extensions of their mother countries. The later years of the 19th century saw the transition from
"informal imperialism" (<color=#3366CC>hegemony</color>) by military influence and economic dominance, to direct rule (a revival of colonial
<color=#3366CC>imperialism</color>) in the <color=#3366CC>African continent</color> and <color=#3366CC>Middle East</color>.
During the socioeconomically optimistic and innovative decades of the <color=#3366CC>Second Industrial Revolution</color> between the 1870s
and 1914, also known as the "<color=#3366CC>Beautiful Era</color>", the established colonial powers in Asia (United Kingdom, France,
Netherlands) added to their empires also vast expanses of territory in the <color=#3366CC>Indian subcontinent</color> and <color=#3366CC>Southeast Asia</color>.
Japan was involved primarily during the <color=#3366CC>Meiji period</color> (1868–1912), though earlier contacts with the Portuguese,
Spaniards and Dutch were also present in the <color=#3366CC>Japanese Empire</color>'s recognition of the strategic importance of European
nations. Traditional Japanese society became an industrial and militarist power like the Western <color=#3366CC>British Empire</color> and the
French Third Republic, and similar to the <color=#3366CC>German Empire</color>.

At the close of the <color=#3366CC>Spanish–American War</color> in 1898 the <color=#3366CC>Philippines</color>, <color=#3366CC>Puerto Rico</color>, <color=#3366CC>Guam</color> and <color=#3366CC>Cuba</color> were ceded to the
<color=#3366CC>United States</color> under the terms of the Treaty of Paris. The US quickly emerged as the new imperial power in <color=#3366CC>East Asia</color>
and in the <color=#3366CC>Pacific Ocean area</color>. The Philippines continued to fight against colonial rule in the <color=#3366CC>Philippine–American War</color>.
By 1913, the <color=#3366CC>British Empire</color> held sway over 412 million people, of the world population at the time, and by 1920, it
covered 35500000 km2, of the Earth's total land area. At its apex, the phrase "the empire on which the sun never sets"
described the British Empire, because its expanse around the globe meant that the sun always shone on at least one of
its territories. As a result, its political, <color=#3366CC>legal</color>, <color=#3366CC>linguistic</color> and <color=#3366CC>cultural</color> legacy is widespread throughout the Western world. In
the <color=#3366CC>aftermath of the Second World War</color>, decolonizing efforts were employed by all Western powers under <color=#3366CC>United</color>
<color=#3366CC>Nations</color> (ex-<color=#3366CC>League of Nations</color>) international directives.
Most of the colonized nations received independence by 1960. Great Britain showed ongoing responsibility for the
welfare of its former colonies as member states of the Commonwealth of Nations. But the end of Western colonial
imperialism saw the rise of Western <color=#3366CC>neocolonialism</color> or economic imperialism. Multinational corporations came to offer
"a dramatic refinement of the traditional business enterprise", through "issues as far ranging as national sovereignty,
ownership of the means of production, environmental protection, consumerism, and policies toward organized labor."
Though the overt colonial era had passed, Western nations, as comparatively rich, well-armed, and culturally powerful
states, wielded a <color=#3366CC>large degree of influence</color> throughout the world, and with little or no sense of responsibility toward the
peoples impacted by its multinational corporations in their exploitation of minerals and markets. The dictum of <color=#3366CC>Alfred</color>
<color=#3366CC>Thayer Mahan</color> is shown to have lasting relevance, that whoever controls the seas controls the world.
During the <color=#3366CC>Cold War</color>, a new definition emerged. Earth was divided into three "worlds". The <color=#3366CC>First World</color>, analogous in
this context to what was called the West, was composed of NATO members and other countries aligned with the United
States.

The Second World was the <color=#3366CC>Eastern bloc</color> in the Soviet <color=#3366CC>sphere of influence</color>, including the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color> and <color=#3366CC>Warsaw Pact</color>
countries like Poland, Bulgaria, Hungary, Romania, <color=#3366CC>East Germany</color>, and Czechoslovakia.
The Third World consisted of countries, many of which were <color=#3366CC>unaligned with either the west or the east</color>; important
members included India, Yugoslavia, <color=#3366CC>Finland</color> (Finlandization) and Switzerland (Swiss Neutrality); some include the
<color=#3366CC>People's Republic of China</color>, though this is disputed, since the People's Republic of China, as communist, had friendly
relations—at certain times—with the Soviet bloc, and had a significant degree of importance in global geopolitics. Some
Third World countries aligned themselves with either the US-led West or the Soviet-led Eastern bloc.
A number of countries did not fit comfortably into this neat definition of partition, including Switzerland, Sweden, Austria,
and <color=#3366CC>Ireland</color>, which chose to be neutral. Finland was under the Soviet Union's military sphere of influence (see FCMA
treaty) but remained neutral and was not communist, nor was it a member of the Warsaw Pact or Comecon but a
member of the EFTA from 1986, and was west of the <color=#3366CC>Iron Curtain</color>. In 1955, when Austria again became a fully
independent republic, it did so under the condition that it remain neutral; but as a country to the west of the Iron Curtain,
it was in the United States sphere of influence. Spain did not join NATO until 1982, seven years after the death of the
authoritarian <color=#3366CC>Franco</color>.
The 1980s advent of <color=#3366CC>Mikhail Gorbachev</color> led to the end of the Cold War following the <color=#3366CC>dissolution of the Soviet Union</color>.
Modern definitions
The exact scope of the Western world is somewhat subjective in nature, depending on whether cultural, economic,
spiritual or political criteria are employed. It is a generally accepted Western view to recognize the existence of at least
three "major worlds" (or "cultures", or "civilizations"), broadly in contrast with the Western: the <color=#3366CC>Eastern world</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Arab</color>
and the <color=#3366CC>African</color> worlds, with no clearly specified boundaries. Additionally, <color=#3366CC>Latin American</color> and Orthodox European
worlds are sometimes either a sub-civilization within Western civilization or separately considered "akin" to the West.
Many anthropologists, sociologists and historians oppose "the West and the Rest" in a categorical manner. The same
has been done by Malthusian demographers with a sharp distinction between European and non-European family
systems. Among anthropologists, this includes <color=#3366CC>Durkheim</color>, Dumont, and <color=#3366CC>Lévi-Strauss</color>.
Cultural definition
The Oxford English dictionary noted that the earliest use of the term "Western world" in the English language was in
1586, found in the writings of William Warner.
In modern usage, Western world refers to <color=#3366CC>Europe</color> and to areas whose populations largely originate from Europe,
through the <color=#3366CC>Age of Discovery's</color> imperialism.
In the 20th century, Christianity declined in influence in many Western countries, mostly in the European Union where
some member states have experienced falling church attendance and membership in recent years, and also
elsewhere. <color=#3366CC>Secularism</color> (separating religion from politics and science) increased. However, while church attendance is
in decline, in some Western countries (i.e. Italy, Poland, and Portugal), more than half of the people state that religion is
important, and most Westerners nominally identify themselves as Christians (e.g. 59% in the United Kingdom) and
attend church on major occasions, such as Christmas and Easter. In the Americas, Christianity continues to play an
important societal role, though in areas such as Canada, a low level of religiosity is common due to a European-type
secularization. The <color=#3366CC>official religions</color> of the United Kingdom and some Nordic countries are forms of Christianity, while
the majority of European countries have no official religion. Despite this, Christianity, in its different forms, remains the
largest faith in most Western countries.
Christianity remains the dominant religion in the Western world, where 70% are Christians. A 2011 Pew Research
Center survey found that 76.2% of <color=#3366CC>Europeans</color>, 73.3% in <color=#3366CC>Oceania</color>, and about 86.0% in the <color=#3366CC>Americas</color> (90% in Latin
America and the Caribbean and 77.4% in Northern America) described themselves as Christians.
Since the mid-twentieth century, the west became known for its <color=#3366CC>irreligious</color> sentiments, following the <color=#3366CC>Age of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Enlightenment</color> and the <color=#3366CC>French Revolution</color>, <color=#3366CC>inquisitions</color> were abolished in the 19th and 20th centuries, this hastened the
<color=#3366CC>separation of church and state</color>, and <color=#3366CC>secularization</color> of the Western world where unchurched <color=#3366CC>spirituality</color> is gaining more
prominence over organized religion.
Certain parts of the Western world have become notable for their diversity since the late 1960s. Earlier, between the
eighteenth century to mid-twentieth century, prominent western countries like the United States, Canada, Brazil,
Argentina, Australia, and New Zealand have been once envisioned as homelands for <color=#3366CC>whites</color>. <color=#3366CC>Racism</color> has been noted
as a contributing factor to Westerners' colonization of the <color=#3366CC>New World</color>, which makes up much of the geographical West
today.
Countries in the Western world are also the most keen on digital and televisual media technologies, as they were in the
postwar period on television and radio: from 2000 to 2014, the <color=#3366CC>Internet</color>'s <color=#3366CC>market penetration</color> in the West was twice that
in non-Western regions.
Economic definition
The term "Western world" is sometimes interchangeably used with the term <color=#3366CC>First World</color> or <color=#3366CC>developed countries</color>,
stressing the difference between First World and the <color=#3366CC>Third World</color> or <color=#3366CC>developing countries</color>. This usage occurs despite
the fact that many countries that may be culturally Western are developing countries – in fact, a significant percentage
of the Americas are developing countries. It is also used despite many developed countries or regions not being

culturally Western (e.g. <color=#3366CC>Japan</color>, <color=#3366CC>Singapore</color>, <color=#3366CC>South Korea</color>, <color=#3366CC>Taiwan</color>, <color=#3366CC>Hong Kong</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Macao</color>). <color=#3366CC>Privatization</color> policies
(involving government enterprises and public services) and <color=#3366CC>multinational corporations</color> are often considered a visible
sign of Western nations' economic presence, especially in Third World countries, and represent a common institutional
environment for powerful politicians, enterprises, trade unions and firms, bankers and thinkers of the Western world.
Other views
A series of scholars of civilization, including <color=#3366CC>Arnold J. Toynbee</color>, <color=#3366CC>Alfred Kroeber</color> and Carroll Quigley have identified and
analyzed "Western civilization" as one of the <color=#3366CC>civilizations</color> that have historically existed and still exist today. Toynbee
entered into quite an expansive mode, including as candidates those countries or cultures who became so heavily
influenced by the West as to adopt these borrowings into their very self-identity. Carried to its limit, this would in
practice include almost everyone within the West, in one way or another. In particular, Toynbee refers to the
intelligentsia formed among the educated elite of countries impacted by the European expansion of centuries past.
While often pointedly nationalist, these cultural and political leaders interacted within the West to such an extent as to
change both themselves and the West.
The <color=#3366CC>theologian</color> and <color=#3366CC>paleontologist</color> <color=#3366CC>Pierre Teilhard de Chardin</color> conceived of the West as the set of civilizations
descended from the Nile Valley Civilization of <color=#3366CC>Egypt</color>.
The idea of "the West" over the course of time has evolved from a directional concept to a sociopolitical concept, and
has been temporalized and rendered as a concept of the future bestowed with notions of progress and modernity.
Bedouin
The Bedouin, Beduin, or Bedu (Arabic: badw, singular badawī) are pastorally semi-nomadic Arab <color=#3366CC>tribes</color> who have

historically inhabited the desert regions in the <color=#3366CC>Arabian Peninsula</color>, <color=#3366CC>North Africa</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Levant</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Mesopotamia</color>

(<color=#3366CC>Iraq</color>/<color=#3366CC>Kuwait</color>). The Bedouin originated in the <color=#3366CC>Syrian Desert</color> and <color=#3366CC>Arabian Desert</color> but spread across the rest of the <color=#3366CC>Arab</color>
<color=#3366CC>world</color> in <color=#3366CC>West Asia</color> and <color=#3366CC>North Africa</color> after the spread of Islam. The English word bedouin comes from the Arabic
badawī, which means "desert-dweller", and is traditionally contrasted with hādir, the term for sedentary people. Bedouin
territory stretches from the vast deserts of North Africa to the rocky ones of the <color=#3366CC>Middle East</color>. They are sometimes
traditionally divided into tribes, or clans (known in Arabic as ašāir; or qabāil ), and historically share a common culture
of herding camels, sheep and goats. The vast majority of Bedouins adhere to <color=#3366CC>Islam</color>, although there are a small number
of Christian Bedouins present in the <color=#3366CC>Fertile Crescent</color> until 21st century.
Bedouins have been referred to by various names throughout history, including Arabaa by the Assyrians (ar-ba-ea),
being a nisba of the noun Arab, a name still used for Bedouins today. They are referred to as the Arāb in <color=#3366CC>Arabic</color>. While
many Bedouins have abandoned their nomadic and tribal traditions for a modern urban lifestyle, others retain traditional
Bedouin culture such as the traditional ašāir clan structure, traditional music, poetry, dances (such as saas), and many
other cultural practices and concepts. Some <color=#3366CC>urbanized</color> Bedouins organise cultural festivals, usually held several times
a year, in which they gather with other Bedouins to partake in and learn about various Bedouin traditions—from poetry
recitation and traditional sword dances to playing traditional instruments and even classes teaching traditional tent
knitting. Traditions like <color=#3366CC>camel riding</color> and camping in the deserts are still popular leisure activities for urban Bedouins
who live near deserts or other wilderness areas.
Society
A widely quoted Bedouin adage is "I am against my brother, my brother and I are against my cousin, my cousin and I
are against the stranger" sometimes quoted as "I and my brother are against my cousin, I and my cousin are against
the stranger." This saying signifies a hierarchy of loyalties based on the proximity of some person to oneself, beginning
with the <color=#3366CC>self</color>, and proceeding through the immediate family as defined by male kinship, and then, in principle at least, to
an entire genetic or linguistic group (which is perceived as akin to kinship in the <color=#3366CC>Middle East</color> and <color=#3366CC>North Africa</color>
generally). Disputes are settled, interests are pursued, and justice and order are dispensed and maintained by means
of this framework, organized according to an ethic of self-help and collective responsibility (Andersen 14). The
individual family unit (referred to as a tent or bayt) usually traditionally comprised three or four adults (a married couple
plus siblings or parents) and any number of children.
Bedouin tribes were not controlled by a central power, like a government or empire, but rather were led by tribal chiefs.
Some chiefs exercised their power from oases, where merchants would organise trade through the territory controlled
by the tribe. The structure of Bedouin tribes was held together by shared feelings of common ancestry rather than by a
tribal chief atop the hierarchy.
The Bedouins' ethos comprises courage, hospitality, loyalty to family and pride of ancestry. Bedouin society typically
revolved around traditional honor codes of the Bedouin, and Bedouin systems of justice, such as the well known
bisha'a, or ordeal by fire, a well-known Bedouin practice of lie detection.
Traditions
Herding
<color=#3366CC>Livestock</color> and herding, principally of goats, <color=#3366CC>sheep</color> and <color=#3366CC>dromedary camels</color> comprised the traditional livelihoods of
Bedouins. These were used for meat, dairy products, and wool. Most of the staple foods that made up the Bedouins'
diet were dairy products.
Camels, in particular, had numerous cultural and functional uses. Having been regarded as a "gift from God", they were
the main food source and method of transportation for many Bedouins. In addition to their extraordinary milking
potentials under harsh desert conditions, their meat was occasionally consumed by Bedouins. As a cultural tradition,
camel races were organized during celebratory occasions, such as weddings or religious festivals.
Some Bedouin societies live in arid regions. In areas where rainfall is very unpredictable, a camp will be moved
irregularly, depending on the availability of green pasture. Where winter rainfall is more predictable in regions further
south, some Bedouin people plant grain along their migration routes. This proves a resource for the livestock
throughout the winter. In regions such as western Africa, where there is more predictable rainfall, the Bedouin practice
transhumance. They plant crops near permanent homes in the valleys where there is more rain and move their
livestock to the highland pastures.
Oral poetry
Oral poetry is the most popular art form among Bedouins. Having a poet in one's tribe was highly regarded in society.
In addition to serving as a form of art, poetry was used as a means of conveying information and <color=#3366CC>social control</color>.
Bedouin poetry, also known as nabati poetry, is often recited in the vernacular dialect. In contrast, the more common
forms of Arabic poetry are often in <color=#3366CC>Modern Standard Arabic</color>.
Raiding or ghazw
The well-regulated traditional habit of Bedouin tribes of raiding other tribes, caravans, or settlements is known in Arabic
as ghazw.
History
Early history
Historically, the Bedouin engaged in nomadic herding, agriculture and sometimes fishing in the Syrian <color=#3366CC>steppe</color> since
6000 BCE. By about 850 BCE, a complex network of settlements and camps was established. The earliest Arab tribes
emerged from Bedouins.
By the time of the Roman Empire's establishment, the Bedouin national identity had been established and they were
recognizable as a single people with often warring "families, clans, and tribes". A major source of income was the
taxation of caravans and tributes collected from non-Bedouin settlements. They also earned income by transporting
goods and people in caravans pulled by domesticated camels across the desert. Scarcity of water and of permanent
pastoral land required them to move constantly.
The Moroccan traveller <color=#3366CC>Ibn Battuta</color> reported that in 1326 on the route to <color=#3366CC>Gaza</color>, the Egyptian authorities had a customs
post at Qatya on the north coast of <color=#3366CC>Sinai</color>. Here, Bedouin were used to guard the road and track down those trying to
cross the border without permission.
The <color=#3366CC>Early Medieval</color> grammarians and scholars seeking to develop a system of <color=#3366CC>standardizing</color> the contemporary
<color=#3366CC>Classical Arabic</color> for maximal intelligibility across the <color=#3366CC>Arabophone</color> areas, believed that the Bedouin spoke the purest,
most conservative variety of the language. To solve irregularities of pronunciation, the Bedouin were asked to recite
certain poems, whereafter consensus was relied on to decide the pronunciation and spelling of a given word.
Ottoman period
Historically, the nomadic Bedouin tribes engaged in frequent inter-tribal <color=#3366CC>warfare</color>, conducting seasonal <color=#3366CC>raids</color> (known as
ghazu) against rival clans for access to scarce pasturages and water resources. One notable example was the
long-standing rivalry between the Shammar and Anizah tribal confederations across northern Arabia and the Syrian
Desert. During the late 18th century, these conflicts, together with the rise of the Wahhabi movement, contributed to the
migration of a major Shammar faction under the Al Jarba family across the Euphrates into Upper Mesopotamia, where
it later emerged as a dominant tribal force.
A plunder and massacre of the Hajj caravan by Bedouin tribesmen occurred in 1757, led by Qa'dan al-Fayez of the
Bani Sakher tribe (modern-day Jordan) in his vengeance against the Ottomans for failing to pay his tribe for their help
protecting the pilgrims. An estimated 20,000 pilgrims were either killed in the raid or died of hunger or thirst as a result
including relatives of the sultan and Musa Pasha. Although Bedouin raids on Hajj caravans were fairly common, the
1757 raid represented the peak of such attacks which was also likely prompted by the major drought of 1756.
Under the <color=#3366CC>Tanzimat</color> land reforms of 1858, a new Ottoman land law was issued, which offered legal grounds for the
displacement of the Bedouin (<color=#3366CC>Turkish</color>: Bedeviler). As the Ottoman Empire gradually lost power, this law instituted an
unprecedented land registration process that was also meant to boost the empire's tax base. Few Bedouin opted to
register their lands with the Ottoman Tapu, due to lack of enforcement by the Ottomans, illiteracy, refusal to pay taxes
and lack of relevance of written documentation of ownership to the Bedouin way of life at that time. Some scholars,
such as Nora Elizabeth Barakat, believe the displacement of the Bedouin had its roots in events even earlier than the
1858 land reforms, for example in an 1844 Anatolia-specific decree recognizing the "tribe" as a formal unit of
administration. The goal of these early reforms was to weaken local Bedouin magistrates and limit what she terms as
"rural mobility", the ability of these local Bedouins to, independently of the Ottoman state, accumulate wealth through
the wheat trade and other means.
At the end of the 19th century, Sultan <color=#3366CC>Abdülhamid II</color> settled Muslim populations (<color=#3366CC>Circassians</color>) from the <color=#3366CC>Balkans</color> and the
<color=#3366CC>Caucasus</color> among areas predominantly populated by the nomads in the regions of modern Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, and
Palestine, and also created several permanent Bedouin settlements, although the majority of them did not remain. The
settlement of non Arabs in the traditionally Bedouin areas was a big cause of discontent. This became even more
severe because every Arab tribe, including the settled ones, have ancestry as a Bedouin.
Ottoman authorities also initiated private acquisition of large plots of state land offered by the sultan to the absentee
landowners (effendis). Numerous tenants were brought in order to cultivate the newly acquired lands. Often it came at
the expense of the Bedouin lands.
In the late 19th century, many Bedouin began transition to a semi-nomadic lifestyle. One of the factors was the
influence of the Ottoman authorities who started a forced sedentarization of the Bedouin living on its territory. The
Ottoman authorities viewed the Bedouin as a threat to the state's control and worked hard on establishing law and
order in the <color=#3366CC>Negev</color>. During the <color=#3366CC>First World War</color>, the Negev Bedouin initially fought with the <color=#3366CC>Ottomans</color> against the
<color=#3366CC>British</color>. However, under the influence of British agent <color=#3366CC>T. E. Lawrence</color>, the Bedouins switched side and fought against
the Ottomans. Hamad Pasha al-Sufi (died 1923), Sheikh of the Nijmat sub-tribe of the Tarabin, led a force of 1,500 men
who joined the Ottoman raid on the Suez Canal.
In <color=#3366CC>Orientalist</color> historiography, the Negev Bedouin have been described as remaining largely unaffected by changes in
the outside world until recently. Their society was often considered a "world without time". Recent scholars have
challenged the notion of the Bedouin as 'fossilized,' or 'stagnant' reflections of an unchanging desert culture. Emanuel
Marx has shown that Bedouin were engaged in a constantly dynamic reciprocal relation with urban centers. Bedouin
scholar Michael Meeker explains that "the city was to be found in their midst."
At the time of <color=#3366CC>World War I</color>, a Qays Bedouin tribe from Harran, not far from <color=#3366CC>Urfa</color>, settled in Lüleburgaz in <color=#3366CC>East Thrace</color>
under their last Sheikh Salih Abdullah. It is said that this tribe was originally from Tihamah.
In the 20th century
<color=#3366CC>Ghazzu</color> was still relevant to the Bedouin lifestyle in the early 20th century. After a 1925 stay with Sheikh Mithqal
Al-Fayez of the Bani Sakher, William Seabrook wrote about his experience of a ghazzu from the Sardieh tribe on
Mithqal's 500 Hejin racing camels. The ghazzu was intercepted by Mithqal when he was notified about the Sardieh
tribe's intentions from a man from the Bani Hassan tribe, who rode continuously for over 30 hours to reach Mithqal
before their plot matured. Mithqal, using the information, prepared a trap for them, which resulted in the imprisonment
of one of the Sardieh warriors. William notes that although the warrior was a prisoner, he was nonchalant and was not
treated aggressively, and that the ghazzu wasn't a war, but a game in which camels and goats were the prizes.
In the 1950s and 1960s, large numbers of Bedouin throughout Midwest Asia started to leave the traditional, nomadic
life to settle in the cities of Midwest Asia, especially as hot ranges shrank and populations grew. For example, in <color=#3366CC>Syria</color>,
the Bedouin way of life effectively ended during a severe drought from 1958 to 1961, which forced many Bedouin to
abandon herding for standard jobs. <color=#3366CC>West Asian</color> and <color=#3366CC>North African</color> states pushed the Bedouin toward settlement
through sedentarization. This process was endorsed by the <color=#3366CC>Arab League</color> and the <color=#3366CC>United Nations</color>, who saw Bedouin
lifestyles as “backward." Some Bedouin were also voluntarily drawn to sedentary lifestyles by a desire for improved
standards of living.
Governmental policies pressing the Bedouin have in some cases been executed in an attempt to provide service
(schools, health care, law enforcement and so on—see Chatty 1986 for examples), but in others have been based on
the desire to seize land traditionally roved and controlled by the Bedouin.
Scholars have questioned to what extent Bedouin were “detribalized” by sedentism. Donald B. Cole, for instance, wrote
that Bedouin people retain social tribal lineages, but shed their former tribal political, economic, or legal structures when
permanently settling.
In the 21st century
Gulf States and their tourist industries have revived or invented certain Bedouin traditions including <color=#3366CC>falconry</color>, <color=#3366CC>horse</color> and
<color=#3366CC>camel races</color>, and pearl-diving, in an attempt to curate national histories and cultures, often in an <color=#3366CC>orientalist</color> manner.
To reconnect with their own heritage, some Bedouin have begun breeding white <color=#3366CC>doves</color>, while others have learned skills
in <color=#3366CC>falconry</color>.
In different countries
Saudi Arabia
The <color=#3366CC>Arabian Peninsula</color> was one of the original homes of the Bedouin. From there, they started to spread out to
surrounding deserts, forced out by the lack of water and food. According to tradition, Arabian Bedouin tribes are
descendants of two groups: Qahtanis, also known as Yaman, who originate from the mountains of Southwestern
Arabia, and claim descent from a semi-legendary ancestral figure, Qahtan (often linked to the biblical Joktan), and
Adnanis, who originate in North-Central Arabia and claimed descent from Adnan, a descendant of the Biblical <color=#3366CC>Ishmael</color>.
A number of Bedouin tribes reside in Saudi Arabia. Among them are Anazzah, Juhaynah, Shammar, al-Murrah, Mahra,
